body:
South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS) will qualitatively evaluate the shareholder engagement activities of its external asset managers and incorporate the results into manager selection and fund allocation and withdrawal decisions. The move represents a sweeping overhaul of a stewardship oversight system that has been effectively dormant for eight years since the Stewardship Code was adopted in 2018. The NPS plans to unveil "Stewardship Code 2.0" in the first half of next year.

The Ministry of Health and Welfare held a briefing on the NPS fund's stewardship activities on the afternoon of the 14th at the Korea Exchange conference hall in Yeouido, Seoul. Approximately 200 executives and staff from 105 listed companies in which the NPS has invested attended. This marks the first time the Stewardship Responsibility Committee has convened portfolio companies in one venue.

Lee Yeon-im, chair of the Stewardship Responsibility Committee, defined the NPS as "an investor, not a regulator," emphasizing that "your companies must generate profits and pay substantial dividends to shareholders for the NPS to become stronger." As of the end of 2025, the NPS is a heavyweight in South Korea's capital markets, holding stakes of 5% or more in 269 domestic companies.

The centerpiece of the briefing was the strengthening of the evaluation framework for external asset managers. In July, the NPS adopted a stewardship compliance monitoring system following a resolution by the Fund Management Committee. The structure involves checking compliance with 12 detailed items across seven principles, compiling a report, and disclosing it through the Stewardship Responsibility Committee.

The new initiative is a qualitative assessment. The NPS will evaluate how well external asset managers adhere to the NPS's stewardship principles and how appropriately they handle conflicts of interest, capturing the qualitative level of their shareholder value enhancement efforts in the report. From next month through November, the NPS will conduct document reviews and on-site inspections, with plans to link the results to external manager selection and fund allocation and withdrawal decisions.

"Until now, there has been virtually no substantive monitoring of asset managers' stewardship activities," Lee said. "Going forward, we will properly monitor them and reflect the findings in investment decisions."

Lee also disclosed six priority management areas that the NPS actually examines in its engagement with companies: whether a reasonable dividend policy has been established; whether executive compensation limits are linked to business performance; concerns over legal violations such as embezzlement, breach of duty, or unfair support; cases where persistent opposition to specific agenda items has not led to improvement; and whether risk management systems for climate change and industrial safety are in place.

On executive compensation, Lee stressed that "the point is not that performance-based pay is large per se, but whether it is properly linked to business performance." The implication is that the NPS has no choice but to vote against proposals to raise compensation limits for executives whose companies are posting losses or showing no clear performance.

For director appointments, Lee explained that the NPS looks at past voting behavior on the board rather than preferences for specific individuals. The key criterion is whether a candidate has a track record of participating in decisions that destroyed corporate value.

Responding to views that the NPS has not been sufficiently active in shareholder engagement, Lee reaffirmed the confidentiality principle. "What we deal with is sensitive corporate information that could affect stock prices," she said. "Disclosing individual matters concerning specific companies could send the wrong signal to the market." The explanation is that because the process is not visible externally, the NPS may appear passive.

Lee did, however, acknowledge practical limitations. Engagement with priority management companies is supposed to conclude within two years in principle, but in practice deadlines are sometimes exceeded. "We look at three things: establishing a policy, disclosing it, and complying with it," she explained. "If only two of the three have improved, we cannot say the issue has been resolved, nor is it easy to escalate to a more active form of engagement."

During the Q&A session following the briefing, questions poured in about the NPS's voting criteria following three rounds of Commercial Act amendments. Particular attention was focused on the criteria for judging cases where companies seek to hold or dispose of treasury shares on an exceptional basis, now that share buybacks and cancellations have become the norm.

An NPS official presented two criteria. First, the NPS has voted against cases where amendments to articles of incorporation regarding treasury share holdings or disposals could be passed solely with the votes of the largest shareholder and related parties, without minority shareholder consent. Second, consistency between the purpose of the treasury share acquisition at the time of purchase and the purpose of disposal. If treasury shares bought for stock price stabilization are disposed of for other purposes, such as employee bonuses, the NPS would view this as a breach of the promise to shareholders.

With cumulative voting set to become mandatory next year for listed companies with assets of 2 trillion won (approximately $1.5 billion) or more, questions were also raised about the NPS's vote allocation criteria when board seats are contested. The NPS responded that it would first exclude candidates with disqualifying factors, then comprehensively consider board activity records and the validity of shareholder proposals.

In February, the NPS expanded its pre-disclosure of voting decisions from companies where it holds a stake of "10% or more" to "5% or more." As a result, the number of companies subject to disclosure increased from 61 to 265. Both the evaluation of external asset managers and the expansion of voting disclosure are seen as measures to make the NPS's exercise of shareholder rights more transparent and proactive.

Hyun Soo-yeop, First Vice Minister of Health and Welfare, said, "I hope this briefing will serve as an opportunity to enhance mutual understanding between the NPS as an investor and the companies it invests in, and ultimately contribute to the long-term development of companies and the stable enhancement of fund returns."
